And so the voice that is heard asks not, “Whom shall I send for myself?” but “Whom shall I send for us?” (Isaiah VI, 8). “Understand, O reader, all that is implied here ... Solomon intended to express the same idea in the verse, ‘Draw me after you, and we shall run.’” This shows that the one who sends and the one who is sent stand at the same degree at the moment of the prophetic mission.

Other thinkers had already developed this theme. Moses ibn Tibbon, for example, in his commentary on the Song of Songs, interpreted the kiss as communion with the Intellect. And Joseph ibn Kaspi writes: “When a human being knows the greatness [of the divine acts], his intellect unites with what it understands and becomes one with it.

“Solomon, inspired by the Holy Spirit, said, ‘Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth’ (Song of Songs 1:2). In the same sense it is written, ‘They dwell at the mouth of God’ (Numbers IX, 18). This is the kiss of the intellect, the only true kiss: not the kiss of the lips, but the kiss of the mouth, the ultimate desire of lovers.” The divine visions of Ezekiel would likewise be interpreted as a communion of Intellects equivalent to prophecy.

Such texts bring into sharper relief something we have already had occasion to say about the identification of the Active Intellect with the Holy Spirit among the philosophers and theosophers of Islam. This identification does not mean that the Spirit has been reduced to reason, as certain Western interpreters have been too quick to claim. Here the philosopher is raised to the rank of prophet, and their union in the act of complete understanding makes the Angel and the soul a single being composed of two.

In its highest form, the act of knowing is not expressed through the abstract language of general concepts, as it is in our theories of knowledge. This act of knowing, which is communion with spiritual universes, is the “kiss of the seraph,” accompanied softly by the Song of Songs. Other spiritual seekers, the Fedeli d'amore, spoke not of the seraph but of Madonna Intelligenza, Lady Intelligence.

In neither case are we dealing with metaphor, allegory, an abstraction given human form, or a general concept. We are dealing with the vision of an essence in its own individual form. For the spiritual world, above the abstract concepts of logic, possesses its own concrete nature and its own individuality, with forms that cannot be perceived unless we possess the faculty of metaphysical imagination. Prophetic philosophy grants this faculty its rightful place by describing how the Angel's light flows simultaneously into the philosopher's intellect and the visionary's power of imagination.

This is why it fell to a theosopher like Suhrawardi, in his visionary writings, to lead the heroes of the heroic epic toward the spiritual knighthood of the mystical epic (see above, Book II). When “doctrine becomes an event of the soul,” the theosopher perceives that event in Isaiah's vision, as did the Jewish theosopher just quoted; in the Grail narrative of Kay Khosrow, as Suhrawardi did in the account we examined earlier; or in a vision of the Imam, as so many Shiite theosophers have done.

Prophetic philosophy and the mystical epic advance together; each is bound to and connected with the other. From their convergence arises a spiritual knighthood reaching across the entire world shaped by the phenomenon of the Holy Book. Its divine service, through which humanity continues to exist, can be expressed only through visionary narratives and epics of the soul—not through general theories or abstract ideologies. This is why the prophets' visions and the mystical epics call for the same kind of interpretation as the spiritual interpretation of the Holy Book.

And this is how we must read our own medieval Western mystical epic: the cycle of the Holy Grail. Only when we understand it in this way does the Grail epic disclose the secret of its spiritual knighthood. To bring this knighthood together with the companions of the Hidden Imam would be to realize the ideal assembly foreshadowed in Goethe's unfinished poem.

We have seen precisely such a meeting anticipated in the mystical narratives of Suhrawardi, the Shaykh al-Ishraq, which initiate the reader into the secret of his “Oriental theosophy”—that is, into the way of living it inwardly. This meeting draws together all the “guardians of the Logos,” those of the East and those of the West, on paths converging toward one another.

There is something significant here—have we paid sufficient attention to it?—in the fact that at the very time of Suhrawardi, the idea of a single knighthood embracing East and West was taking definite form in the work of Wolfram von Eschenbach. Of course, that would be merely a chronological coincidence, an entirely external one.
But Qazi Sa'id Qommi has taught us that true simultaneity must be sought in the Malakut, the spiritual world. And it seems that there, indeed, we may find it.

Recent studies have rightly emphasized that the Arthurian Round Table seems to be an emanation of the Table of the Grail, from which it receives all its light. It is for this reason alone that Galahad's journey to the “Spiritual Palace of Sarras” passes through the Arthurian Round Table. What matters most about that table is its symbolic meaning: its correspondence with the structure of the cosmos as a whole. It represents the roundness of the cosmos.

Here we may think of the spirit of the School of Chartres, the influence of commentaries on Plato's Timaeus, and the Hermetic writings (see above, Book II): the World Soul extending from the center to every part of the body of the cosmos and embracing it entirely; a single, solitary, circular heaven, “capable, by its own power, of remaining within itself without needing anything else.” We might already say that the Table of the Grail is the soul of the Arthurian Round Table.

In any case, the cosmic correspondence expressed by the latter is perfectly in keeping with the manifestations of the pleroma of the Twelve that we have encountered here: the fullness of the Twelve Imams, whose invisible dwelling places are symbolized by the twelve signs of the zodiac; the esoteric hierarchy whose totality corresponds to the 360 degrees of the sphere; the fullness of the Twelve gathered around the Friend of God of the High Country; and the twelve Rosicrucian knights in Goethe's poem.

It seems to us, then, that we must begin with this cosmic correspondence if we are to understand how, in Wolfram's work, the castle of the Grail is transformed into an entire world: the “world of the Grail” itself. This world and its knights must necessarily be situated in a kind of space that we recognize as a quarta dimensio, a fourth dimension—or, better still, as the Malakut.

For reasons that have compelled us throughout this study to speak of the imaginal, we refuse to call this space “imaginary.” The fact that this world is “everywhere and nowhere” is precisely what the Persian expression Nâ-kojâ-âbâd, coined by Suhrawardi, means. This is the defining character of the “eighth clime,” the mundus imaginalis, or the world of Hurqalya: it has its own real location, but that location cannot be defined by our geographical coordinates.

The appearances of the Hidden Imam and his companions have likewise led us back to this ubi, this “where” which, in relation to our earthly space, is an ubique, an “everywhere.” It is right to say that the world of the Grail, while impossible to locate geographically, is a sovereign world with frontiers to defend. Its chosen members may enter it “from the Arthurian world of forests and rivers,” and they may leave it to undertake missions.

I believe that the world of the Hidden Imam and his companions, and indeed the world of the mystical epic generally, correspond to this description. The quest for the Imam as the “Soul of the soul” is a journey like that of Parsifal “toward this world situated outside ordinary space.” One enters this world because one belongs to it by birthright.
But we must remember that everything here takes place in the “eighth clime,” to which all the landscapes, persons, and actions belong.

Thus, when we speak of a “birthright,” we mean birth into this world of the eighth clime—the world of the Grail. This is the birth of the gnostic, the person awakened to spiritual knowledge. It gives him not only the right but also the duty to return to the world to which that birth has made him belong. Such is the meaning of the entire gnostic epic, of the “Hymn of the Pearl,” and of the Iranian mystical epic: the story of the exile (ghorbat) whose conclusion is a return to his own people. The return to the world of the Grail, the return to the mystical Sinai, and the return to the Green Island of the Imam all have this same meaning.

This is why the knighthood whose world is symbolized by the Round Table forms a universal spiritual elite, drawing its members from “pagan lands”—by which our old authors meant the world of Islam—as well as from Christendom. The world it represents is a “perfect world,” a pleroma, a complete spiritual order. One enters it by casting off every attachment and ambition belonging to the ordinary, secular world. This is the very meaning of tajrîd, the stripping away of worldly attachments, in Sufi spirituality.

The bonds of brotherhood joining its companions make them a fellowship comprising the spiritual elite of humanity. In its hierarchy, and in deciding who its heroes are, it recognizes only spiritual qualifications. This is also the distinctive rule of the world of Hurqalya. It therefore appears that the emergence of the world of the Grail, with its entirely distinctive place and order of existence, is what makes possible the meeting and coherence of the two other worlds present in Wolfram's work: the world of the Arthurian cycle and that of Eastern knighthood.

In saying this, we are not concerned with techniques of literary creation, but with the order of being that determines a world's structure and the way that world is perceived. When Wolfram's epic welcomes the knighthood of Islam, its inner movement mirrors that of the mystical epic through which Suhrawardi brings the Hellenized Magi of ancient Iran back into Islamic Persia.

Throughout Wolfram's writings, the theme recurs of a “pagan” knighthood equal in brilliance and worth to Christian knighthood, “except for baptism.” The finest representatives of this Eastern knighthood—that is, the knighthood of Islam—are considered equally worthy of a place at the Round Table.

In Wolfram, however, it is precisely through the joining of these two forms of knighthood that a spirituality emerges which belongs to the very idea of knighthood and is therefore shared by the knights of Christendom and Islam. It is true that, in the service of the Grail understood as a personal service to God, the knight's relationship with God is much more that of a vassal to his lord than that of a sinner to his redeemer.

We have already encountered an outstanding example of this relationship, and of the ideal governing it, in the struggle of the Fravartis on behalf of Ohrmazd. We also recalled earlier the judgment of Eugenio d'Ors, who rightly perceived that the conception of the spiritual world underlying Zoroastrian ethics leads of itself to the idea of an order of knighthood.

And we have shown that this is precisely the conception inspiring the ethics and mysticism of fotowwat: the preeternal covenant it implies, recalled in the definition given by the Third Imam, and the designation of Ali as the “supreme knight”—lâ fatâ illâ 'Alî, “there is no knight but Ali.” As for Wolfram, it has been said that he was a layman speaking to laypeople. Certainly.

But the world of the Grail already knows nothing of the ecclesiastical hierarchy or the apostolic succession of the Roman See. And what Wolfram presents to laypeople is precisely the ideal of knighthood, because he himself is a knight.

Yet to be a knight, though it is not to be a cleric, is no more simply to be an ordinary layperson. The meeting between the Friend of God of the Oberland and Rulman Merswin belongs to this same spiritual line of development: the age of the cloisters has passed, and the new message leads to the founding of the Knights of Saint John of the Green Island.

The ethics of spiritual knighthood, of which we have just recalled several examples, is expressed among the Shiite theosophers as the covenant and bond between rabb and marbûb: between the sovereign lord and his faithful servant.

What is involved is an essential relationship between the two, an essential coexistence. The first term therefore cannot refer to the Deus absconditus, the hidden God who transcends every attribute and every relation. Rather, it refers to the theophanic Figure of that hidden God, the Face shown to the faithful servant—and that Figure is the Imam.

The bond between rabb and marbûb is fundamentally a covenant of faithfulness. To betray this covenant is not to destroy what the rabb is in himself—the Imam remains the Imam even when he is ignored and rejected. It is to destroy the relationship outside which rabb and marbûb cannot exist for one another. And for the faithful servant, this means destroying himself by allowing the world they constitute together to be destroyed. The Imam dies for him only if he himself dies to the Imam. This is why the Fravartis did not betray Ohrmazd.

The same ethics is shared by every form of spiritual knighthood: the Templars of Wolfram's epic, the knights of Goethe's poem, and the knights of the Imam. Once again, we may borrow from a Kabbalistic writer words that express exactly what governs the ethical relationship we have in mind: “God needs his presence to dwell in the Temple.” “In all their afflictions, he himself was afflicted” (Isaiah LXIII, 9).

This is also why anyone who refuses to see the presence of God as making Wolfram's Parsifal a theological and mystical poem thereby admits an inability to read it as every narrative of initiation and every mystical epic must be read: in the way one reads the Holy Book. Here we may follow the same instruction Suhrawardi gave for reading the Quran: each person should read it as though it had been revealed for that person's own particular case.

The events related in Wolfram's epic take place in the mundus imaginalis. The battles fought there, the weapons used, the celebrations held—all these events are so many affirmations or sudden irruptions of the imaginal world into the poet's imaginative consciousness. We have learned that such appearances announce, by their very nature, the elevation into the imaginal world of a doctrine that has become an event of the soul and within the soul. It is therefore the task of spiritual interpretation to disclose their esoteric meaning.

But this must not be done by descending again to the level of the logical clarity of doctrinal concepts. It must be done by following the path along which doctrine is transformed into event, without ever denying the reality of that event.

This is why, despite what has sometimes been said, there is no opposition between the eschatological meaning of the world of the Grail—as the heavenly Jerusalem, the City of God—and the mystical meaning of the Quest. It would be absurd to set against one another, on the one hand, an eschatological meaning concerning the final union of the community with God, or even the “assumption” of history into a higher reality, and, on the other, a mystical meaning of the Quest grounded in a doctrine of personal union with God within “human time”. Such an artificial opposition seems inspired by an underlying assumption that gives priority to the collective from the outset.

There can be no final union of the community without the successful completion of the personal Quest undertaken by each of its members. Nor is that personal Quest pursued within “human time.” It unfolds precisely within “knightly time,” which is why the Quest is itself eschatological and brings about its own eschatological fulfillment.
The time of each Quest is one portion, one quantum, of “knightly time.” Yet knightly time unfolds “between times.”
We can speak of an “assumption of history” only in the sense of a passage into the time of the Malakut, the spiritual world.

But this time breaks through the chronological time of irreversible history because it is, in its very essence, a mysterium liturgicum, a liturgical mystery. Galahad was real and truly completed his Quest in the ecstatic death he experienced at Sarras. And yet Galahad's adventure remains forever about to happen. It does not end when the reader reaches the last page of the book. Knightly time is brought to a close neither by a date in chronology nor by the final page of a book.

In this sense, it is the time of the ghaybat, the occultation. This is why we have already drawn a parallel between the occultation of the Imam and the concealment of the Holy Grail. The Imam's occultation does not end with the founding of the sanctuary of Jam Karan or with the last page of his sacred biography. We have seen that his hidden history continues throughout the period of his occultation. Similarly, the history of the Grail did not end with its concealment following its “return to the East.”

But the Grail's secret history can continue only by breaking, each time, into the course of collective, outward history. Each of its manifestations, like each appearance of the Imam, breaks the fabric of “dark and dense time,” because it raises the visionary into another order of time, one whose repetitions and reversibilities belong to a liturgical mystery. Here lies the very secret of a knighthood that persists incognito in this world, with members in East and West alike.

A liturgical mystery: many indications suggest precisely this. It is on the day of Pentecost that the young Galahad, the “awaited” knight, the “Desired One,” appears at King Arthur's court and sets out from there upon the Quest of the Grail. We have also already noted how confidently several Shiite theosophers identify the “awaited” Imam with the Paraclete—the divine Comforter or Spirit promised in the Gospel (see also below).

The liturgical mystery in which the knights of West and East meet invisibly thus appears as the very mystery of Pentecost. It is also a mystery whose ceremonial unfolding was contemplated by the princess Narkes (Narcissus), mother of the Twelfth Imam, in the dream visions we related earlier. Within the precincts of an ideal temple of Holy Wisdom, Hagia Sophia, she saw Christ with his twelve apostles, and the Prophet with his eleven Imams, ascend together the steps of a single pulpit of light.

But before Narkes could finally see the Twelfth Imam, her mystical bridegroom, she had first to be initiated in a dream by Fatima and to accomplish the tawhîd, the acknowledgment of the One beyond all oneness. And now we read in Wolfram that Feirefiz, Parsifal's brother, could not see the Grail until he had received baptism. Only then, too, did his marriage to the Grail queen, Repanse de Joie, become possible. These are not “scientific” findings, but subtle and suggestive resonances.

Everything happens as though one voice were sounding the theme of a fugue on a great organ, and another voice were answering it by reversing that theme. Whoever can hear these resonances may perhaps discern in the first voice the counterpoint called forth by the second. Episode by episode, the entire fugue would then unfold to completion.
But that completion is precisely the “mystery of Pentecost,” and only the Paraclete has the mission of unveiling it.
3. The Twelfth Imam and the Reign of the Paraclete

Our study of Shiite prophetology has led us to recognize two convictions that sustain the faith of the Shiite spiritual seeker. The first is that the cycle of walayat, the cycle of initiation through the “Friends of God,” corresponds perfectly to the cycle of prophecy. Just as each prophet (nabi) manifests an aspect of the eternal prophetic Reality, so each Friend of God manifests, in his own particular way, the perfection of the Perfect Human Being whose final Seal is the presently Hidden Imam—the Seal of walayat.

It follows that each Friend of God stands in relation to the final Seal of walayat, the Twelfth Imam, just as each prophet stands in relation to the Seal of prophecy. This first conviction implies a second, which gives the followers of Shiite spirituality a distinctive inner strength. They are called to realize mystically, in their most intimate depths, a relationship with the Imam as the Seal of spiritual initiates, analogous to the relationship of the prophets with the Seal of prophecy.

This personal manifestation is, in a sense, the fruit of the celebrated hadith upon which the very concept of the Friends of God is founded: “The sages of my community correspond to the prophets of Israel.” The masters warn us that by these sages we must understand the “Sages of God” ('âlimân-e rabbânî), the “theosophers”—those whose knowledge of the divine mysteries comes to them as a divine gift, through inward unveiling (kashf) and direct inspiration, rather than through the dialectical instruction of a human teacher.

By establishing this correspondence, the hadith declares that every mystical theosopher has a prophetic calling. Certainly, it applies in the first instance to those who are the Friends of God in the highest sense and who, precisely for that reason, are the Guides who initiate others into spiritual meaning: the Twelve Imams.

But we also know that the Imams communicated their own walayat to their followers by initiating them into their spiritual knowledge. And because that teaching came from the Imams, it was divine initiation rather than a tradition passed down merely by human beings.

The essential distinction has already been explained to us: in the person of the Imam, who is the source of walayat for the entire mystical hierarchy, even at levels invisible to ordinary humanity, walayat has the nature of the sun. In the persons of his followers, who become Friends of God through him, walayat has the nature of the moon.

Yet the illumination bestowed upon them by the Imam's light is no less complete. For this light is wholly present in each Perfect Being whom it invests, in the sense that it illuminates the entirety of that person's being.

This explains why a number of these spiritual figures have felt themselves to be, in truth, unique beings. Several of them, in both the recent and distant past, have experienced themselves as the “Seal of Initiation” (khâtim al-walâyat). Such was the certainty Ibn Arabi experienced, as we have noted, following a symbolic dream vision.

A master of Shiite Sufism such as Shamsoddin Lahiji invites us to understand how all of them could have been sincere, and in what sense all of them spoke the truth. In other words, he explains how every initiate may be the Seal of Initiation, and every Friend of God the Seal of the Friends of God.

“Through the perfection of their vision,” he says, “the gaze of each of them came to rest upon the pure and eternal Reality of walayat, beyond their personal individuality. If we understand their claims without the rigidity of religious bigotry, those claims show that each of them, at his own particular moment, was the most perfect being of that moment, and that each then possessed the eminence of the supreme spiritual pole—the polar function (qotbîyat) proper to the eternal Muhammadan Reality.”

Yet this event takes place, and has its validity, only within the secret world of souls, within the Malakut. It is not an event that becomes publicly known and establishes itself as a fact of outward history. To manifest within oneself, in anticipation, the Seal of the Initiates is to bring about within oneself, and for oneself, the parousia—the appearing or manifestation—of the Imam. This does not in any way suspend the time of occultation (ghaybat) or proclaim that it has ended. Rather, it hastens its ripening.

For it is in this way that the Night of esotericism progresses—the cycle of walayat, the Night of Destiny, “in which the Angels and the Spirit descend”—toward the dawn that will be the Imam's manifestation for all. Here we recognize the profound meaning of the cycle of walayat and the very force that animates Imami spirituality in Iran. After the Seal of the Messengers, humanity has no further prophet to await. The majority have consequently devoted themselves with fanatic zeal to guarding the closed letter of revelation.

But without the complementary idea of the Seal of walayat, embodied in the Imam who is still to come, the idea of the Seal of prophecy becomes the sign of a human tragedy: humanity shuts itself, without hope, inside a past that has no future.
The Shiite understanding of the cycle of Initiation, by contrast, transforms the meaning of this closure by bringing forth from it the necessity of Renewal.

What is therefore required of every follower of Shiite spirituality is the quest for the Hidden Imam. For the follower, this means allowing the Imam to reveal himself within the secrecy of one's own consciousness—to “bring the Hidden Imam to birth” within oneself.

And this, precisely, is the “history” of the Hidden Imam throughout the period of the Great Occultation: a history of souls and a history unfolding within souls. It allows us to sense what is shared by Brother Marcus's quest at Montserrat, the final message of the Friend of God of the High Country, and the dream vision of the princess Narkes. This anticipation of the final Seal within each follower is what gives rise to the eschatological philosophy and spirituality characteristic of Shiism. For this sense of the ultimate fulfillment expresses the living relationship between the faithful follower and the Hidden Imam, the Twelfth Imam.

As we have already emphasized, this relationship must be understood in such a way that the manifestation of the Hidden and Awaited Imam is not simply an event that will happen one fine day. To await the Imam means that the Imam's manifestation depends, in a corresponding measure, upon each follower.

For ultimately—and this is how a distinguished shaykh once explained to me the meaning of one of his own books—the deepest significance of the ghaybat, the occultation, is that human beings have themselves hidden the Imam from their own sight. They have made themselves incapable or unworthy of seeing him. We might express this by turning a familiar account around: sacred history tells us that God banished Adam from paradise, but the mystic discovers that it was Adam—humanity—who banished God from paradise. And that is the reality of the Infernum, of Hell.

Hell is this night of human consciousness, and it is this night that makes the hidden, inner meaning of revelation necessary. Only when the Resurrector appears is the night dispersed, because then every secret meaning of every Revelation becomes manifest: the triumph of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation.

At that point, there will be no more esotericism, because nothing will remain hidden. This is the thought inspiring a great many traditional texts, of which we can recall only a few here. The Shaykhi school has admirably clarified, even in our own time, the profound meaning of the Imam's occultation: human beings themselves have become incapable of seeing him.

But we must emphasize that, from a very early period, the Imamis were already quoting and meditating upon a statement of the First Imam as a confirmation of their faith. For that statement had foretold the ordeal they would undergo among skeptics declaring: “God's Proof (Hojjat) has departed; the Imamate has disappeared; it is all over.” The Imam had announced: “Certainly, the Earth will never be deprived of a Proof of God.

“But human beings will be blind, unable to see him, because of their darkness, their excesses, and the crimes they commit against themselves”—that is, against their own souls. The Imam offered his disciples the story of Joseph as an example. Joseph stood there before his brothers, yet none of them recognized him. The great mystical poet Attar would say that every one of us, at every moment, commits the crime of selling a Joseph. So it is today: the Imam sees each of us, but no one sees him.

And this night is so deep, so desperate, that escaping from it requires the radical act of going into exile. The same shaykh mentioned above recalled to me a hadith declaring that a day will come when it will no longer be possible even to pronounce God's name in this world.

On occasion, disciples of the Fifth and Sixth Imams asked them about the meaning of a tradition whose words carry a deeply moving resonance, and which we recalled a few pages earlier: “Islam began as a stranger in exile, and it will become a stranger in exile again, as it was at the beginning. Blessed are those who go into exile.”

The two Imams gave essentially the same answer: “When the one among us [the Twelve] who is the Resurrector (Qâ'im) arises, he will proclaim to humanity an entirely new Call (da'wat, the Greek kerygma) to something entirely new, just as the Messenger of God proclaimed his Call”.

Those exiles who are declared blessed are the ones who leave behind a religion defined by law and social order in order to join the spiritual worship to which the Imam calls them. To the extent that these exiles hear that Call here and now, the night of esotericism advances toward the dawn of the Resurrector, and the Imam's manifestation is already being accomplished through each of his followers. This is what is meant by the mystical growth of the Perfect Human Being.

The relationship between the event still to come—the Final Manifestation—and the event that is already taking place within the secret depths of human hearts is therefore essentially a process of inward realization. It gives the idea of the Imam's manifestation its present and practical meaning by showing us that the outward event is conditioned by the inward event. Such is the teaching of the masters of Shiite spirituality.

We have already quoted here the famous hadith in which the Prophet announces the manifestation of the last Imam, a declaration repeated afterward from Imam to Imam: “If the world had only one day left to exist, God would lengthen that day until a man of my descendants appeared. His name will be my name, his kunya [honorific name] will be my kunya. He will fill the Earth with harmony and justice, just as it will until then have been filled with violence and oppression.”

Sayyed Haydar Amoli interprets this hadith through ta'wîl, returning it to its inner meaning. The Prophet announces that the Imam “will fill the Earths of all hearts—those Earths which are as numerous as human hearts—with tawhîd and gnosis, after they have been devastated by shirk, the unconscious fragmentation of the divine and of being.” For this is indeed what the manifestation of the last Imam means.

The texts describe the tumultuous struggle that he and his companions wage against the Adversaries, but that tumult is the very struggle being fought now within human hearts. And the struggle will continue until every heart has recognized the meaning of the theophanies, until all recognize that wherever they turn, “there is the Face of God” (3:109), because God alone truly is, because divine Oneness is precisely what makes the multitude of divine manifestations possible, and because the multiplicity of beings is the very essence and universe of the One.

Another very great master of Sufism, Sa'doddin Hamuyah (thirteenth century), whom we have quoted more than once already, declared: “The Hidden Imam [the Mahdi] will not appear until people are capable of understanding the secrets of tawhîd even in the straps of his sandals.”

By this he meant the esoteric significance of bearing witness to the One and to divine Oneness: that beneath all the different divine forms, one and the same divinity is manifested. It is this same secret that Haydar Amoli perceived in the beautiful poem by Ibn Arabi with which he opened and closed one of his major works: “My heart has become capable of every form ... I profess the religion of love, and whichever direction its mount may take, love is my religion and my faith” (see above, Book IV, p. 189).

Ultimately, this secret is gathered together in the person of the Awaited Imam, just as it was in the person of the hero Humanus in Goethe's poem. For the Imam is the Perfect Human Being, the Human Being in the fullness of his spiritual reality.

Sa'doddin Hamuyah's saying, then, means that the Imam will appear only when, one follower after another, human beings have become capable of understanding what his very person announces. For the hidden reason why he remains concealed is none other than humanity itself. This saying is complemented by another: “When the Hidden Imam appears, through him stones, plants, and animals will begin to speak.”

We shall return below to an Ismaili saying that echoes it: when a thing comes alive, it becomes a threshold to the spiritual world. Here, too, lies the secret of the “Night of Destiny.” We have seen how Imam Hasan al-Askari asked the venerable Hakima to recite over the newborn Imam the Qur'anic verses that announce this Night.

All of this, together with Lahiji's commentary, allows us to grasp the full meaning of the Imam's appearance and reign. The justice with which, according to every tradition concerning him, he will fill the world is not the prize in a struggle over social arrangements: it is the salvation of the cosmos. That is what gives meaning, generation after generation, to the efforts of those who are the “companions of the Imam.”

The Perfect Human is a theophany (mazhar), a visible manifestation of the supreme divine Name that gathers all the Names into itself. In his person he gathers together all the manifestations of the divine Names. This alone makes the human being “God's representative on earth,” and it is this humanity in its fullness that is identified with the Hidden Imam. The task of this divine representative is to uncover and bring to light the divine Name entrusted to each being, hidden in the sleep of seemingly lifeless nature or in human unawareness. As the perfect theophany, the Perfect Human enters into the secret of the divine manifestation within beings.

Through him, each being's hidden potential for perfection becomes actual: its secret, its inner meaning, is disclosed. Stones, plants, and animals will reveal their hidden meaning; so will every doctrine and every human religion. Divine Unity will thus reveal its very essence through the multitude of its manifestations. This is what the Coming—the Parousia—means. When the Imam's justice “levels” all opposition, it does so through the multiplicity of theophanies that disclose the secret of their unity. A spiritual teaching concerned with hidden meanings will naturally understand the renewal of all things as the unveiling of what lies concealed within them.

But Lahiji reminds us that we can know something perfectly only by becoming that thing. A mystic's verse says: “Become resurrection, and then behold resurrection.” The same truth is hinted at when it is said that God can be known only through God. This is why the resurrecting Imam, as Perfect Human and perfect theophany, is called the Initiator without equal, the “Seal of Initiation,” the Seal of walayat—the spiritual bond of guardianship and initiation. He places that Seal upon each of the Friends of God.

Against this background, the declaration of faith made by Shi'i spiritual philosophers who identify the Twelfth Imam with the Paraclete promised in John's Gospel takes on its full weight and meaning. There is nothing surprising about this identification once we recall how readily both Twelver Shi'i and Ismaili authors turn to the Gospel of John. We have already examined texts that make this identification.
Let us bring them together one last time, beginning with the scriptural passages on which they rely.

First comes the verse in John: “The Paraclete, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26; compare 14:16 and 15:26–27). Then comes this Qur'anic verse (61:6): “Jesus son of Mary said: Children of Israel, I am God's messenger to you, confirming the Torah that is in your hands and announcing a messenger who will come after me, whose name will be Ahmad”—a name understood as “most praised,” equivalent here to the Greek periklytos. A common Muslim interpretation holds that Parakletos, meaning comforter or consoler, is a distortion of periklytos, “most praised,” the Greek equivalent, on this account, of the Arabic Ahmad or Muhammad.

According to that interpretation, Christians made this alteration to prevent John's verses from being read as foretelling the Seal of the Prophets. In this reading, the promised Paraclete is the Prophet Muhammad himself. Shi'i interpretation, however, applies the title to the Twelfth Imam. The shift presents little difficulty. In announcing the Imam of Resurrection as his own descendant, the Prophet speaks of him almost as another self: “His name will be my name, and his byname will be my byname.”

More importantly, the promised Paraclete will not proclaim a new sacred Law. He will reveal the inward, hidden meaning of all the earlier Laws. Muhammad brought a new Law; the Twelfth Imam's mission is to reveal the meaning concealed within revelation. Historians of religion will notice that this is precisely the role the Manichaeans attributed to the prophet Mani, whom they too regarded as the Paraclete. Mani came above all to “resolve” what had remained unresolved: he was “the Solution.”

Let us return, then, to the passage in which Haydar Amoli comments on the Prophet's words announcing the Imam of Resurrection: “Even if only one day remained…” Having quoted them, he adds: “This is what Jesus alluded to when he said: ‘We bring you the outward wording of Revelation (tanzil). As for its spiritual interpretation (ta'wil), the Paraclete (al-Faraqlit) will bring that to you at the end of this age.’ Now, in Christian terminology, the Paraclete is the awaited Imam, the Mahdi. The underlying meaning of the Prophet's words is therefore this: the Paraclete will bring you the spiritual meaning and true understanding of the Qur'an, just as I have brought you its revealed wording (tanzil) and its literal explanation.

“For the Qur'an has an outward and an inward aspect, a literal explanation and a spiritual interpretation. [...] As the Prophet also said: ‘The Qur'an has an outside and an inside; that inside has an inside of its own, and so on, through seven hidden depths—seven inward meanings.’” This text makes the identification unmistakable: for Haydar Amoli, the Paraclete promised by Jesus is the Twelfth Imam, now invisible, whose coming was foretold by Muhammad. It is for the Imam-Paraclete, as both Jesus and Muhammad are said to have declared, to reveal the hidden meaning of Revelation. The very principle of Shi'i spiritual interpretation is therefore inseparable from the idea of the Paraclete.

Another great Shi'i spiritual philosopher whom we have already encountered, Ibn Abi Jumhur (fifteenth century), comments on the same saying of the Prophet—“Even if only one day remained…”—in words taken here from a longer discussion: “When Jesus said, ‘We bring you the outward wording of Revelation; as for its spiritual interpretation, the Paraclete will bring that to you,’ his words refer to Muhammad, son of Imam Hasan al-Askari. He is the Imam of this age, recognized as the Mahdi, for the Paraclete, in Christian terminology, is Muhammad the Awaited One”—that is, the Twelfth Imam. “This is also what Kamal al-Din Abd al-Razzaq Kashani means in his spiritual interpretation of the three letters alif, lam, mim.

“The letter alif refers to the divine Self (dhat Allah), the first principle of being (awwal al-wujud). The letter lam refers to the Active Intelligence, also called Gabriel, which stands at the centre—the middle point—of being (awsat al-wujud), as being flows from its Principle and pours forth to its furthest limit. The letter mim refers to Muhammad, the awaited Imam, who is the end of being (akhar al-wujud), the one through whom the cycle of being reaches completion. The end rejoins the beginning: the Seal is set in place.” Here again, the Seal of the cycle of being and the cycle of walayat is the Paraclete promised by Jesus. He is the Seal destined to bring our aeon, our present world-age, to its close.

As I said earlier, these statements by Twelver Shi'i thinkers have their counterpart in the work of an Iranian Ismaili spiritual philosopher, Abu Yaqub Sijistani (fourth/tenth century). In a chapter especially characteristic of the openness these thinkers showed toward the hidden meanings of other religions, Sijistani seeks to demonstrate that the inward meaning of the Christian Cross's four arms is the same as that of the four words making up the profession of God's oneness, the shahada.

He writes: “Jesus announced to his people that when the Imam of Resurrection—of whom Jesus himself was a symbol—laid bare, without any veil, the inner truths hidden beneath the structures of the revealed religions, whose very framework rests upon these truths, human beings would recognize them and could no longer deny them. [...] Jesus announced to his people that it would be easy for the Imam of Resurrection and his companions to draw out the spiritual meaning of every thing. [...] For it is reported that on the Night of Destiny light pours forth. At that moment walls, trees, and every lifeless body worship this light. This symbolizes the power of the Imam of Resurrection, the Qa'im, and his companions.”
